utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Unfortunately, the previous trial in this courtroom had a delayed finish, so we had to start a little late. I understand there may be a matter before the witness comes in. Is that right, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Indeed there is. I feel somewhat embarrassed to keep objecting about something all the time. During the last session yesterday at 1808 we received an e-mail message from the OTP informing us that due to circumstances beyond their control witnesses Bozidar Protic and Goran Stoparic will not be able to appear as witnesses as previously determined on the 23rd of March, and will therefore be struck from the witness list for the weeks to come. And then there is a list of the following ten witnesses, the witnesses coming up now. On this list we have witnesses appearing over the next couple of weeks, their names stated in a summary fashion. I believe this was on the 25th of February, so some seven or eight days ago, that we were facing problems in relation to this, organising our Defence, witnesses being announced, and the order of appearance being changed. You stated in the clearest terms possible the problems being faced by both the Court and the Prosecution, and then we adopted a set of rules determined by the Trial Chamber, that being to prepare for the next witness coming along. Your Honours, I believe the fundamental problem here, in view of all your rulings, since the Pre-Trial Conference we said that there should be a two-week notice served on the Defence about witnesses to appear over the next weeks. I don't think this is a deliberate move on the part of the OTP, but we are facing a number of problems. Specifically, let me share a couple of facts with you. The Defence received notification from the OTP in relation to the week starting on the 2nd of March. We received this notification on the 16th of February, with only two witnesses Bogujevci Fatos and Bogujevci Saranda with 05 hours allotted for each. The Defence can in no way influence the planning procedure nor indeed can we decide who the witnesses will be. We've got a total of two witnesses for that week; I accepted that. Bearing in mind the problems we had on the 25th, we talked to Ms. Kravetz and we determined that Radojkovic had been subpoenaed at some point without the Defence knowing about this; but now he was also placed on that list for the week starting on the 2nd of March. Radojkovic, Bosko, Witness Radojkovic, Bosko his evidence scheduled to last for an hour, this notice is dated 23rd February this year. At the same time the first part of that motion, the OTP informed us that in the week starting on the 9th of March the first witness to appear will be Goran Stoparic followed by K88 followed by K84 followed by Bozidar Protic; and then as I said in relation to the 16th of March week which is what we received yesterday, or rather, on the 2nd of March we see witnesses that are named a while ago: Merovci, Adnan; Bala, Nazalie; Kabashi, Emin; Zyrapi, Bislim; Baraybar, Jose-Pablo. Now what we get is a summary list, there is no breakdown according to weeks. We have one, we have two, and when the actual witnesses will appear, we don't know that. After Saranda Bogujevci, the next witness was Fatos Bogujevci if he doesn't appear then Goran Stoparic would be appearing. This was the OTP's plan for the following week starting on the 9th of March. Now the OTP has informed us they have certain notice on us that K88 would be appearing this week to testify. All of our preparations were based on the OTP's plan for the first reserve witness as it were, and we have been using all our resources to work towards that end; and yet all of a sudden the order had been reshuffled and now we are facing a situation in which we are no longer able to organise ourselves. So these weekly plans of the OTP - and I don't think this is a deliberate subterfuge on their part - have not been consistent. The problem is we, our Defence team, cannot cope with this method. I think we should comply with the Chamber's order on these weekly plans or schedules. We can only prepare for the witness coming up. Now we should be preparing today for Bogujevci, Fatos if Saranda fails to appear. And Fatos was supposed to be the last week appearing this week based on the existing plan. Therefore we're thinking that Stoparic was coming along, and that's what we were preparing for. Things being what they are, we are no longer in a position to make sure our client gets the quality defence that he deserves. The order of witness appearances being shuffled all the time as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner -- I beg your pardon, I didn't see you hiding there out of sight. Ms. Kravetz.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just to address this issue very briefly. The next witnesses who were scheduled to appear are Saranda Bogujevci and Fatos Bogujevci. This hasn't changed. We had already notified the Defence about this order in our e-mail dated the 25th of February which was sent following the discussions we had regarding witness scheduling last week in court. The only changes to this schedule are Goran Stoparic and Bozidar Protic who are no longer being called in the order previously announced. So Witness K88 will now be testifying after Fatos Bogujevci. The reasons why Mr. Stoparic is not being called this week I can discuss them if Your Honours would like more details, but we would have to go into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very briefly we will go to private session, and you can just outline in the shortest fashion.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: And I would just like to indicate that the remaining witnesses will testify in the order that have been notified, so it's K88, K84, and then the witnesses who were just notified in our notification of this Monday. So the only two changes are those two witnesses and for the reasons I have just outlined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would understand the implication of what you have said is that as soon as each of those witnesses is able to be in The Hague it will be proposed to call them?

utterances.speaker: MS. KRAVETZ
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. That's what we propose to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, as you have heard, what has happened is that two witnesses that have been in the list to be called over the next two weeks have had to be dropped from their order in that list because for two different reasons. Neither of those witnesses is able to be in The Hague to be called in the order originally intended. In other respects, the witnesses to be called are still to be called as listed and in the order listed, and the two witnesses, one of whom was to be called shortly, that is, the third witness from now, will not be able to be called until that witness is in The Hague and then the witness will be called. In the Chamber's view, if you recall our discussion a few days ago which you have mentioned, this is just the sort of exigency that can arise and for which all counsel have to be prepared. If the fact that one or two witnesses over the space of a fortnight are not able to be called precisely when indicated, but otherwise the intended list witnesses are being called in the order indicated; if that is the case, in the Chamber's view it is going to be necessary that counsel are in a position to cope with that sort of adjustment in their planning. And if that's presenting some particular difficulty for the way that you are presently managing the preparation of the Defence case, it would, I think, simply mean that you would have to make some adjustment to the way that you are preparing. I don't think we need anything more about it -- say anything more about it at the moment, and we will continue with the witnesses. As counsel are aware, we're actually running behind the expected timetable with this list, so that the absence of two witnesses is not productive of any great disturbance over the space of the next fortnight. And it will be anticipated that at some future time, perhaps even in the next fortnight, one or both of these witnesses will arrive. When that happens, any preparation that the Defence has made for them will be able to be called on so that there should be no difficulty anticipated in dealing with them. If the witness could be called into court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radojkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Radojkovic. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry for keeping you waiting. We had to deal with some other matters. Mr. Djurdjic is in the middle of asking you questions. Mr. Djurdjic -- I beg your pardon. We haven't finished Mr. Neuner. I stopped you to allow you a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radojkovic.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: We stopped yesterday at the point when we were talking about graves at Petrovo Selo. Could you just tell us who pointed out in 2001 where exactly these graves were located.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. I'm not quite sure. There was some debate going on between you and the Defence, and then the Chamber stepped in. I'm not sure what the ruling was. Am I supposed to make any statements about this incident or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, unless I'm mistaken, Mr. Neuner had moved on to a different topic and then you said since he wasn't able to finish it we would be picking up today where we left off yesterday. I think this was discussed yesterday, and it was determined what the circumstances were that the witness would be testifying to. We have something about it in his statement. If we look at the June 2001 note it was stated mistakenly that there were KLA uniforms involved, and then the witness confirmed that indeed there were no uniforms there. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: As I understand it, Mr. Neuner, the graves at this location which you have mentioned, Petrovo Selo, have no relevance to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, they have relevance to this case. I don't want to go in front of this witness into any further details, but somebody 's -- that's the Prosecution's position were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misunderstood yesterday the point of your questioning. Are you pursuing this issue further with the witness today than the question you have asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understood, Your Honours, that after the objections I obtained that I was permitted to pursue that line of questioning, but maybe I misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I understood yesterday that an explanation for what was said to be a mistake in an official note of the witness was that he confused the incident we are concerned with with an exhumation from graves at Petrovo Selo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This is indeed correct, Your Honours, but in the Prosecution's view there were some bodies buried in that very same location which are also relevant for our case but not for the truck incident itself but for another incident. This witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How is it going to assist us to know who told this witness about bodies in a grave at some other place?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understood the witness to mean that he was a crime technician at the time when the exhumation was carried out, and I just wanted to elicit a few facts stemming from this work as a crime technician. And this would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: How does this arise in re-examination, Mr. Neuner?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I believe I'm still in examination-in-chief, Your Honours. I wanted to complete it but it was not possible due to the objections I received yesterday. There is no cross-examination yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I tell you our fundamental difficulty, Mr. Neuner. We proceeded yesterday on the basis of an understanding that we had from you that there was only one relevance to this issue of exhumation, and that is that by mistake a reference to it had been included in a document that is otherwise a document dealing with our case. What you are now advancing is something that no one of us understood yesterday that there is some other relevance of this exhumation or these bodies at Petrovo Selo. Now, if that's the case, has this been the subject of notice to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The 65 ter summary doesn't contain any explicit reference to this place, Your Honours. So if I get an indication from the Chamber, I would then ask no further questions about this, only a question about the KLA uniforms found there and this would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have that indication, Mr. Neuner. We're not happy for you to be pursuing that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I just ask then for how many bodies were exhumed in 2001 at Petrovo Selo while you were a crime technician?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm only focusing on the uniforms, my learned colleague, I need to establish first how many bodies we are talking about to get something -- some information about the uniforms. That's all I'm trying to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no doubt you know this better than I do. When one looks at this question: How many bodies were exhumed? We're going back to the exhumation, aren't we? As far as I'm concerned the only question that would be legitimate is: Did you see the uniforms or didn't you see the uniforms, which I believe has been asked and answered. He confirmed that there were no uniforms and that the statement was mistaken in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the view that you can ask only as to the number of bodies and the number of uniforms, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This is exactly what I tried to do, but I may have omitted before -- Your Honours asked me about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, that's the ruling. Go on and do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I just -- I've omitted one information. Certainly the Defence, through a supplementary information sheet, was put on notice about all the facts I was going to elicit from this witness today, and this supplementary information sheet had been sent, of course, in advance of yesterday's examination-in-chief. But Your Honours asked me for the summary, and in the summary, as I mentioned, there was no indication of Petrovo Selo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ask your question, get your answer, and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, the question was: How many bodies had been exhumed in Petrovo Selo in 2001?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were 16 bodies in one grave and 58, I believe, in the other. As to the exact figure, I'm now unable to remember. There were some problems piecing the bodies together, but what we found would indicate a total of between 70 and 80 bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you personally attended the exhumation of each of these 70 to 80 bodies in Petrovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, from the beginning to the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What clothes, if any, did these 70 to 80 dead persons wore?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian clothes for the most part, but there were some KLA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could you, first of all, give an indication in percentage how many of these 70 to 80 bodies were civilian clothes -- or were in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be easier for me to tell you the number of uniforms that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Take it from this angle, how many persons or bodies wearing uniforms were exhumed?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Six bodies had KLA uniforms on them. Two of these olive-drab with KLA insignia on the armband, and four black KLA uniforms with combat vests - that's how we referred to those. There were another two bodies with civilian trousers and camouflage shirts. One of these bodies had an armband with the flag and coat of arms of the Federal Republic of Germany. Another body had that same short shirt, but in the same spots where the previous body had the flag and the coat of arms of the Federal Republic of Germany this other body that portion had been cut away leaving a blank square there. Two other bodies had civilian clothes but the same type of boots as the uniformed bodies. That's about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Could I just -- because you mentioned now a couple of numbers. Could you just clarify, is it fair to say that ten or less than ten bodies, corpses, wore what you would describe as uniforms or clothes which could form part of combat gear?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that six were certainly wearing complete military clothing with KLA insignia, six; two had those shirts that I have described which need not necessarily mean the same things; and another two who were wearing military boots, but again I'm not sure whether they were civilians or KLA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So I've just counted the figures given in your last answer, we're not talking about more than ten bodies, which could be implicated wearing some military items?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I made the number 14 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: -- to clarify this very point, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I thought it was clear. Six had KLA uniforms, two had -- two of them were olive-drab and four black. Two other bodies had civilian trousers and camouflage shirts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, could you just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two of the bodies had civilian clothes but boots the same as uniformed --

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Witness, could you clarify, are we talking about a maximum of 14 or a maximum of ten persons wearing such items which we could nowadays portray as combat gear?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were ten bodies, I spoke of ten bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You mentioned a couple of times KLA today. Just in general, what did you understand at the time and looking at these 70 to 80 bodies, what did you understand at the time to be the origin wherefrom these persons had come from in the first place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's a very broad question. It is very difficult for me to answer that question just now. You want me to remember what I thought at the time. I knew certain facts at the time. It's not a question of what I thought, so I could not give you an adequate answer to that question. Perhaps you would like to clarify it a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you are using the word "KLA uniform," this suggests to me that they may have come from a certain region within Serbia at the time, and this is all I wanted to ask you for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that such a question is not appropriate. It is asking for guess-work, and my learned friend is expressing his own opinion in an effort to impose it on the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The question should be withdrawn, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this point in time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We now come, Mr. Djurdjic, to your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Radojkovic, my name is Veljko Djurdjic. I'm a member of the Defence team for the accused, Vlastimir Djordjevic. With me today is Ms. Marie O'Leary, and the lead counsel, Dragoljub Djordjevic is absent because he's working on the preparations for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I bid you a good afternoon to all of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: We all speak the same language and everything needs to be recorded in the transcript and to be translated, and if I speed up a little please wait with your answer until the transcript comes to a full stop. And don't let this upset your concentration.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know. You have more experience than I do. I will be asking you about the facts and circumstances that you were aware of at the time of your main testimony here, and when I refer to another period, I will indicate it clearly. And if you don't understand me, please feel free to tell me that and I shall try and make myself clearer and rephrase the question. Let us start with the last question put to you by my learned friend. Let me ask you whether you were aware, at the time, whether you knew that the KLA were prone to wear civilian clothes and commit terrorist actions particularly in inhabited areas?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, I have studied all your statements closely, and I shall try and focus only on some matters which have not been covered so far, in view of the fact that we already have the transcripts and the statements that you gave. Tell me, please, what are you by training?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am a policeman, but later on I completed a course for crime technician. So I'm a policeman with -- and I completed a secondary school of internal affairs plus a seminar on crime techniques.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I didn't manage to establish from 1974 to 1978 where were you working and what was your position?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1974 I started working as a policeman, and I was in -- working in Zajecar for two months. After that I was transferred to the police station in Kladovo; I was a policeman. Then I worked in the analysis service, in the search section; and then I went to Belgrade and Zemun, where I completed my training for a crime technician and this was in 1979. Ever since then, I have been working as a crime technician up until my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me, please, Mr. Radojkovic, in 1999 what was your rank?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Crime technician. I don't remember whether we had ranks, really, in those days, but I was a senior clerk or a sergeant, first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But you weren't wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I worked in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what was your title?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, a senior crime technician. That's what it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you have a separate section for crime techniques?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there were only two of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But you were in charge?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was too small a unit for one to be in charge -- well, I was senior in experience. The other person was Jova Dobric.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be pauses between question and answer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You made a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal in June 2002. Can you tell me in what language you were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were to see now, as certain documents here are considered statements even though they're not statements, I'm in a dilemma as to what you are referring to. And -- I apologise. An official note is here treated as a statement and it is not my statement, but there is another document that is a statement which I made to the Tribunal investigator in 2002. It was translated for me into Serbian, and I signed the document in English, and that document was later given to me in the Serbian language in 2006. Now have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I do I understand. I do make a distinction between a statement to the Tribunal and a statement according to the criminal law of the Republic of Serbia and official notes drafted in Serbia. In view of the fact that you are a career policeman, we'll come back to that a little later and clear up a few points. Thank you. The last thing you said was that in 2006 you received that statement. Did you receive that statement in the proofing for the trial in the Milutinovic case?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And is it right to say that the written statement that you gave to the Tribunal, you did not receive it in your own language when you signed it for the first time in 2002?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't receive it in English or in Serbian. I signed it in the MUP of Serbia, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But where did you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building of MUP in Makis, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So you made this statement to the investigators of the Tribunal there?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, but this was a very short statement of five sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see the original version of your statement once you signed it? Did you ever see the original version?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. But the contents that I did see is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that that statement has been admitted into evidence as an exhibit as well as the official note that you mentioned, we will go through those documents a little later to see what may not be quite in accordance with what you said. Could you tell me, please, which documents were used by the investigator when you gave your statement for the first time in Belgrade, if any?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain to you that the investigator first came to Kladovo, but I refused to talk to her. We did have a cup of coffee and we had a normal conversation, but we didn't discuss the issue. And then he said that he had the official note which I gave to the Working Group of the MUP. Then he returned to Belgrade, and then in the evening, that very evening, I remember it was a Saturday, they called me up to come to Belgrade on Monday morning; and that is when I made the statement of five or six sentences and I'll explain later which, which parts are from that statement. So I had very little contact with the investigators. They presented to me the official note of the Working Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right in saying that you saw the official note for the first time compiled by the Working Group when it was shown to you by the investigators of The Hague Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it in his laptop. I was the 38th in order among those statements. I didn't really read it. I said I wasn't interested in what was written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'm saying is that the -- the conversation you had with the Working Group was on the 14th of May, 2001, and you saw the note compiled about it for the first time in the laptop of the Tribunal investigator?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And actually I was put in a fait accompli position.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me go on and ask you, did you see who compiled the official note?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- the signatory of the official note was the Working Group, but these are all my friends, my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How many of them signed that official note?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I saw it, no one signed it; but I do know who compiled it, who drafted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you present when this note was being drafted?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How then do you know who drafted it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was drafted by those who had this interview with me -- at least that is what I assume. After all, that is the Working Group, and they said that they were the Working Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, let me not count your years of service, but during those years of service, did you ever see an official note that was not signed?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that that is in contravention of all the rules of police procedure in those days and today?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are probably right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You spent many years of your life working as a police officer. Would you not agree that the probative value of such an official note in Serbia is non-existent. The only thing it can be used for is operative work in pre-trial proceedings and may be used by an investigating judge while conducting an investigation during the pre-trial stage?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that it has no probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that such official notes must be separated from any documents used at trial and may never be used during the actual trial?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are put in separate envelopes and I myself have come across instances of this being the case, these official notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, which reminds me, the established practice of Serbia's police was as follows: Whenever a statement is taken from anyone at all for any reason whatsoever, although there is no procedural importance that attaches to this, it has to be handwritten; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Possibly an official could put together a statement and then have it signed by the interviewee. Yet again, this statement would have no probative value at trial whatsoever, would it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There would be a note saying that the statement has been read back to the witness, the witness identifies the statement as his own, and thereby signs it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you this: Why did the Working Group not want you to make a statement about particular topics or indeed allow you to write up your own statement based on your recollection concerning incidents that they were looking into?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was interviewed by the Working Group, I was facing a number of health issues and was in fact in hospital in Kladovo. Perhaps the conditions were not there for a written statement to be taken or made, but I was not aware of them taking any statements from the other 20 people involved, mere official notes, that's all I know about. I did go to the MUP later on and I did not make a statement about that, not according to the proper procedure under the Law on Criminal Procedure over in our country. I never made a statement like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right when I say that no one was informed as to what note, precisely, was drafted based on the interviews?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you yourself informed about the substance of the note that was produced following your interview before you were eventually shown it?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you were at the health clinic. Was it a sudden problem or a problem that you had been suffering from for a long time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some chest pain but nothing more serious than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know why I'm asking you this? Because the note says that of those four days you were kept at the health clinic because they were suspecting the possibility of a stroke; am I right, there is no truth to this at all?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back in 1985 I suffered a hemiparesis which was a convulsion of my facial muscles, but if I had suffered a stroke I probably wouldn't be here today talking to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I right to state that the official note was inaccurate in that respect then?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't accurately drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Well, the inaccuracy would have been what they said about the stroke, the suspicion of a stroke. Mr. Radojkovic, let us try to clarify the dates back in 1999. Am I right to say that the first indication you ever had of the truck in the Danube came on the 5th of April, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was the 5th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's try to clarify this because sometimes we see the 4th quoted as the right date, but in most of your statements it is the 5th of April and that's where the situation evolved from?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that there is a little problem about that in these statements, but we can take it day by day. Why these references to the 4th and then some other references to the 5th, I think there was some sort of an internal problem as the dates were recorded, but I think it's of no consequence at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us try to clear up about how the truck was hauled up. On the 5th of April you -- one day you spoke to Mr. Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Since some time had already elapsed you secured a truck which was some 30 metres from the river-bank, you tied a length of rope to a tree, you placed a plastic mark to mark the place where it was. Your job was finished for the day?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's how I think it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That was the first day. The next day you made sure there was a pulley there which you used to haul the truck back to the river-bank; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the edge of the water itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Which is the same thing as pulling it up to the river-bank; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there's a recurring problem here which I believe you have noticed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely why I'm asking. And then day three you get a crane or a pulley that is even bigger, and you haul the truck out of the water and ashore. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right. Again, we pulled it out of the water before we could get it ashore.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on day four you got this truck and put it on to a vehicle which then you used to transport it further up on to the road; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Day three, day four -- well, first we hauled the truck out of the water altogether, and then we put it on this vehicle. If you want me to explain, I can tell you why the procedure was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let's take it one step at a time. I know why the procedure worked like this, but please tell me if I'm right. Once you had pulled out the first 30 bodies, the truck was on the river-bank already, was out of the water. And then when the next truck was supposed to come, you placed it on these rails, on this vehicle, and you took it further up; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to day one. There was the diver, Mr. Djordjevic. You're standing on the banks of the Danube. He dives into the river. Is this how it worked: He subsequently informed you that there was a Mercedes truck, refrigerator truck, that the windshield was missing, and all the other steps that you took?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, there's something else that I want to know, Mr. Radojkovic. I'm wondering if this was something that happened by accident or not, but it wasn't before you gave evidence in the Milutinovic case in addition to all these facts that I have mentioned. What is stated is that a large stone was placed on the gas pedal; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic, the diver, told me about that, that the gas pedal had a large stone on it to weigh it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But that wasn't there at first. The only thing that was there was the missing windshield in the first note that the Working Group drew up; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure I told them. I'm not sure if they mentioned that subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps think that they simply didn't want to look further into this large stone weighing the gas pedal down, they just lost over that circumstance?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wouldn't go that far. I'm sure I told them and the diver did too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, you are a police officer and you know this is a very important circumstance in an incident like this, a large stone weighing down the gas pedal and a missing windshield and no driver there, the driver is gone, these are material circumstances and would be to any police investigation anywhere in the world. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are certainly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And if you have a group of forensic experts as qualified as those, you would hardly expect them to missing something like that, would you?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you in turn would agree that this is not my problem, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. Thank you. Mr. Radojkovic, nevertheless, before the Milutinovic trial you gave evidence in the Milosevic case. In that trial you also said he had told you that the windshield was missing and that this was a Mercedes refrigerator truck. The OTP were there, the Chamber was there, and I'm not mentioning the experts at all. They were top-notch experts. And then you appearing as a witness, yet no questions about this large stone arising. How come?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one asked me; that's what is probably was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I will have to clear this up now, Mr. Radojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have on our screens exhibit -- Defence Exhibit D002-0227, page 3, line 25. I'm sorry, maybe I misstated the number. 002-0227, Defence exhibit. I have a hard copy available. I apologise for my English. Page 8470, line 25, and 8471, the first seven lines at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: It reads like this, Mr. Radojkovic: [In English] "When you saw that, what happened next? Did you give instructions to anyone to do something or did you investigate in some way ... it was in fact a truck or a lorry? "A. Yes, I did. The diver put on his equipment and dived into the water, and when he re-surfaced, he told me that it was a lorry, that there was no one in the cab, that the front windshield had fallen out, and that it was probably a Mercedes lorry and its trailer box looked like that of a refrigerated lorry." [Interpretation] You've heard that, Mr. Radojkovic, no windshield, no driver, and a Mercedes refrigerator truck, the same thing that was established by the Working Group in its official note; right? The date being the 23rd of July, 2002.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you know why I'm talking to you about this? That same evening, and I see that when I look at your statements, you said that this was a traffic accident involving a truck in the Danube. One of the reasons for you to say that would have been because there was no driver and there was no windshield. If the stone was in the truck back then, being the experienced policeman that you were, you wouldn't have described it as a traffic accident, would you, since there was a large-scale stone weighing down the gas pedal. Would you not agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote up no dispatch that I subsequently sent to Bor. It wasn't me who informed them. My associate Nesa Popovic might have, although I don't believe that. If there was anything that was dispatched, the note probably said that this was probably a traffic accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. And I know that that's what was subsequently dispatched -- whether he wrote it or you is no matter at all. But you have one thing where this is a large-scale stone weighing down the gas pedal and when there isn't that indicates something entirely different, doesn't it? Yet in your first official note and in your evidence in the Milosevic trial you make no mention whatsoever of any stone in the cabin, do you? It is not before 2006 that you mention, for the very first time, this stone?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what I can tell you is the diver told me about that stone weighing down the gas pedal. Why did I not mention that in the Milosevic trial? Why is it a part of the note? I probably didn't think to mention that, and no one probably asked me; but there were a lot of things that I didn't say in the Milosevic trial. There are a lot of things --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Radojkovic, the Prosecutor did ask you. This was your answer to a question from the Prosecutor. It wasn't a free conversation in which you were talking nor did Mr. Milosevic ask you anything. It was -- the Prosecutor asked you what the diver had established, that there was no windshield, no driver, et cetera, but I won't insist. I'll move on. There's another matter that I'd like to ask you about. Were you alone with the diver at the Danube or was someone else there?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just me and the diver.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And where were you before that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that I was at home because it wasn't my shift. This was an extraordinary occurrence and I had to go to work and Mr. Nesa Popovic was always with me in patrolling, and again problems arise. Like all policemen, he had some private business, and he didn't come with me, he went off to do something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but it seems to me, judging by your statement, that you were in town and that you were not at home.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was free, and then the duty person called me to come to work before I was due to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Were you wearing the same clothes?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I took an official vehicle and went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you have your equipment with you when you were there with Djordjevic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. I may have had my camera. We just went to see what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And when you were there for the first time, you didn't take any photographs of the truck?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took photos of the truck on two occasions, so I can't tell you now whether it was the first day when it was submerged in water. I just saw a big box. Nobody knew it was a truck until the diver dived. I just saw the top part of a big box. It could have been a container. And when the diver dived down, he saw that it was a truck; and after that, our activities continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So if on a photograph we see a part of the box, then it was taken on the first day; and if we see more than the top of the box, then it was taken the next day?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And about what time was it when you finished, you and the diver, on that first day?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. It was in the late afternoon. It took time for us to go there and for me to find him then to go home and for him to get his equipment. It was already dusk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said you went back and informed Popovic, et cetera; we don't know who he went on to inform. But did you inform your own duty service about what you found there?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not. I don't think Nesa did either, but we did inform our boss.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And the duty service had already been informed?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a fisherman had reported it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You just said that you informed who, Nesa? Someone else?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said perhaps Nesa informed the duty officer. I said our boss, Milan Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you also inform the chief of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could counsel repeat the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it's time for the technical break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be useful just to get the transcript clear. It was not possible to pick up what you said at line 19: "Did you also inform the chief of the ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, did you inform the chief of OUP Kladovo, Vukasin Sperlic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not, and I'm not sure whether Nesa Popovic did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Djurdjic. We'll have the first break now and resume at 4.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to ask to tender this part of the transcript from the Milosevic trial which we read to the witness, and it was Defence document D002-0227, page 3, line 25, or number 8470 as the transcript page; and page 4 or 8471, lines 1 to 7. It is the part that I read very clumsily in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You read well, Mr. Djurdjic. No need to apologise. The document -- the transcript extract will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D00039, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Let us now digress a little, Mr. Radojkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see exhibit number, of the Prosecution, P00359, please. I didn't say the transcript. It should be a photograph, 00359, Prosecution exhibit, that was the number it was given yesterday -- no, no, I'm sorry, you're quite right. P361. I do apologise. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, you encircled a leg on this photograph, but I truly do not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it possible to zoom so as to make this clearer?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Is this what you meant? Below the box, is that the leg?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- I'm afraid what I have is like a mirror.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness doesn't have the image.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness has encircled and it's been enlarged and we can see well now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you something. So this here is what you circled? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is the left leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you, yesterday on this photograph in eastern Serbia the Prosecutor asked you to circle Belgrade. Am I right that you did so at the request of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the circles I made were at the request of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radojkovic, we've come to the end of the first day. Tell me, were there any other activities at the end of the day when you went to the Danube river-bank for the first time?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, apart from the markings and the information I was given by the diver, that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were any steps taken to secure the crane?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Could the usher please switch off the monitor with my image on it, it's disconcerting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While that's happening, Mr. Djurdjic, I am a little confused. I take it, Mr. Radojkovic, this photograph was taken by you. Was it taken on the first day or the second day that you were at the river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This photograph was taken on the second day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. That was my understanding. I'm not sure whether Mr. Djurdjic thought that it had been taken on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question did not focus on the time the photograph was taken. My problem was that I couldn't see the leg on this photograph, so I wanted it to be cleared up for me and the witness did. When it was enlarged I saw it better, and I'm afraid that my intention was simply to clear that up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, the question was: Who took any steps to secure the crane, if someone did?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the OUP, I think Mr. Sperlic, he organised that with the hydro power-station.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we've now come to the second day. Tell me, how did that day begin for you? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, early in the morning, I went to the site. My colleague, Popovic, was with me then because the hydro power-station starts working at 6.00 a.m., and it had already been organised a previous evening that a crane from the power-station? Should come to the site for us to try and pull out the truck from the Danube. This was quite customary because they would give us the same sort of assistance in the case of traffic accidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I assume you took your equipment as a crime technician that day?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did take my equipment, my camera -- may I just add that the investigating judge of the municipal court in Kladovo was informed about this as well as the municipal public prosecutor, that there was this in the Danube, that there was a truck in the Danube, and that we would be pulling it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the diver come on that second day?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when did he arrive?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he also came early in the morning, but I think he came in his own vehicle, but we had agreed for him to come early in the morning because he is the only one who can tie the pulleys. We needed a diver to pull the lorry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at what time did you actually start pulling the truck out?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This didn't last -- didn't begin much later than we arrived because we had to stop the traffic because there was this large crane on the road, then the diver had to dive and attach the pulleys to the truck, and then the extraction started because the bottom of the Danube there is very muddy, and the diver had to open the door and turn the wheel for the for the wheels to be in a parallel position because of this movement through the mud. So that - let me tell you exactly - about 12.00 it was pulled out roughly to this position that we see on the photograph now, if you still have that photograph. And I can now also explain why I'm confirming this time, because the investigating judge of the municipal court said that we should let him know once we've pulled out the truck, and then he would come, for him not to waste time. And the judge did arrive about 1.00 or 1.30 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I be right to say that while you were doing this the workers from the hydro-electric power-plant had already finished their business and left the scene; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they stayed until that evening, as did the crane. There were about 15 workers from the hydro-electric power-plant. They had to work the ropes and the pulleys. The work involved here is a little risky and peculiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These are allegations from the official note of the Working Group, and that's what led me to conclude that. So you wouldn't say that was an accurate note?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the note is inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Inaccurate. All right. You had a certain fear that the refrigerator truck might be booby-trapped; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: This is the Bor SUP territory, S-U-P; it wasn't your territory. Do they have a specialised team for anti-sabotage work?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't. In the Kladovo area I would be in charge of that kind of business and the same applies to the teams from Bor and from Zajecar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When this fear arose, that was before you opened the rear door of the container. Do you know if the deputy public prosecutor and the investigating judge were there already?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were both there already when the door was opened, and the coroner from the Kladovo medical centre was present too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what about the foot that you saw? Did you sort of push it back into the container and subsequently covered the hole in the door with the tin sheet?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did that beforehand. As soon as I could access the door, I did that. There were about 20 people there and you could see everything from the road, and there was a bus that had been pulled over and all the traffic was stopped. As soon as I could, I pushed it back in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Isn't that slightly peculiar, Mr. Radojkovic?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What, the fact that the foot was sticking out or that I pushed it back in?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The fact that there was a foot sticking out is not strange at all; it's a fact that you found. But you came there as a forensic technician; you were supposed to secure the scene and all the evidence found on the scene. You see a foot sticking out of the container, you push it back and you try to close the hole in the door by applying a tin sheet over it. You thereby altered the crime scene; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, I did alter the crime scene. It would have been highly unpleasant for these workers from the hydro-electric power-plant who are not involved in that kind of work to have to attach ropes to the container and chafe against this foot sticking out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I know murder is most unpleasant, Mr. Radojkovic, but you are not supposed to alter the scene containing any evidence, you are supposed to secure it and not touch the evidence at all?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, under normal conditions that would have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So what was so unusual or abnormal about this situation? Let us try to state the facts: You have a refrigerator truck submerged in the Danube. You think that there is a traffic accident that occurred. You pull it up. You see that a foot is sticking out. What is your inference based on that?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation itself was abnormal. There were the air-strikes and a truck turns up with Prizren licence plates, there is a foot sticking out of the rear of the truck. I did find the situation slightly unusual or abnormal I have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree, but you are a professional forensic technician. Whatever you find on a scene must be nothing out of the ordinary, and you should know full well that you are not supposed to touch anything; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did what I did. I was not called to account for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, at this point in time the only facts that remains is that there was a person in the box before the truck was submerged in the Danube; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, look, I peeped through this hole. I saw a heap of something like a stack of hay inside. It was dark. I couldn't see. I tried to use my torch, so obviously I used this tin sheet to cover up the hole. It wasn't something for the workers of the hydro-electric power-plant to do. They needed someone to deal with these practicalities before they could get on with their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I would like to digress now if I may. At the time, in your area, which is a border area, was there any trafficking going on in terms of people being smuggled across the border, asylum seekers, that sort of thing. Did you perhaps ever experience any such incidents?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, generally speaking the Djerdap lake area is an area that is very good for something like that, and it's much used for these purposes. Just before this happened, perhaps a month before, it was somewhere near Golubovac that a boat had been turned upside down, or rather, was capsized while travelling and some immigrants and asylum seekers drowned. That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the investigating judge arrived, did you inform him of any steps that you previously took? Did you tell him about the fact that you patched up the hole in that door with the screws and the tin sheet?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I told both him and the deputy municipal public prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Am I therefore right to say that they knew that inside the truck's container there was at least one body?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Radojkovic, would I be right to say that in order to have proper judicial procedure one must first make sure that such officials as the investigating magistrate and the deputy public prosecutor be on the scene whenever something like this occurs?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what exactly the Law on Criminal Procedure was that applied at the time. I do believe that at the time we were authorised, following permission being granted by the investigating judge, to start our on-site investigation and get on with our work, and then we were allowed to keep him informed as our work progressed. That was the practice, but this was a road that was adjacent to the River Danube and sometimes vehicles would go flying off the road and into the river. Whenever something like this happened, the judges would tell us to first go there, do our work, get the vehicles out of the water, and then they would shortly be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Radojkovic. Precisely so. An investigating judge may authorise you to carry out an on-site investigation, but you must act upon his permission or authorisation. In this specific instance, he authorised you to take certain steps and to call him as soon as the refrigerator truck was out of the water and somewhere where it could be accessed. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You weren't trying to conceal anything from these judicial bodies or officials and you brought them there immediately so that they could see what exactly was going on?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a single fact was concealed but there were some contradictory things turned up later on but that's a different thing altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Then you opened the door, you, investigating judge, the deputy prosecutor, and your colleague realised that there were a number of bodies inside the truck's container; am I right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigating judge never had a look to begin with; rather, I told him. When the door was opened, everyone withdrew to a distance of 50 to 100 metres and I was the one to actually open the door. I opened the door, I looked to see what was inside, and I shut the door -- or rather, it was like this: I shut the door and subsequently informed the investigating judge of the municipal court, whereupon he replied that this was not something that he would be in charge of, and he left the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the deputy prosecutor, was he present as well?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. You see that the container is aslant, so you must stand on your toes in order to be able to peer into the container because there were those several bodies that were near the door, but most were midway down the -- into the container, as it were, and then towards the bottom. So he had a look in, and the coroner did as well - there was no need, but he's normally involved in procedures such as this one - so he had a look as well, and that was about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So what you are telling me now is that as soon as on day two when you started hauling the refrigerator truck out of the Danube he saw a bit of the rear of the container and you already had a coroner who was on the scene; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, together with the deputy public prosecutor and the investigating judge; that is when Dr. Trajkovic arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: From the health centre; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's a general practitioner who also happens to work as a coroner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, the first day when Djordjevic went into the water he realised that the driver was missing. What sort of pre-emptive measure was this for you to bring a coroner there on day two already without knowing exactly what the situation was inside the truck and whether there was anything else there?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You never asked the question, did you; if you had, I would have answered it so you would know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Please explain.

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the procedure was first initiated to get the truck out of the water, as I said, the diver, Djordjevic, went into the river. He tried to get the wheels back in a parallel position in order to be able to pull the truck out of the river. While the truck was still submerged the diver was out and said, Bole, there is a pair of feet sticking out of the rear. Once the truck was in the shallows, it was easier to see what there was. So he realised that there was a pair of feet sticking out, and he said, What can we do about this? And I said, What can you do about this? And I replied, Let's pull it out like this and then we'll see what we do next. That was the reason that the coroner arrived with the investigating judge and the deputy prosecutor with the entire team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would I be right to say that members or officers of the SUP don't have the power to issue any orders to an investigating judge or, indeed, a deputy prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Quite the contrary, in fact. An investigating judge in situations such as these imparts orders to the police and the police are duty-bound to act upon these?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would I be right to say that the investigating judge present on the scene, although he believed he was not technically in charge, would have had to issue orders to you and subsequently inform the appropriate prosecutor about the fact that there were actions that needed doing without delay?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the investigating judge -- yes, I'm sure about him too, but we informed immediately the district prosecutor in Negotin because this was within his remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, you also subsequently informed the district investigating judge and the district deputy public prosecutor, but he would have had to give you some instructions before they ever arrived. The procedure was in the hands of the investigating judge until he arrived; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's what he said. He said, Shut the door and wait for the public prosecutor and investigating judge who were in charge to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree that this was not a legal step, the one taken by the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm no expert in matters of law myself, but I would tend to agree with you. Particularly if we keep in mind the Law on Criminal Procedure that is in force these days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Given the connotations of this official note, would I be right to say this: Everything that went on with the refrigerator truck, there was no information that was withheld from the judicial organs and the state organs; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Quite the contrary in fact. Everything was done by the book, and the appropriate local prosecutor was immediately informed. For some reason, though, the ball was soon back in the police's court because those other people had said they were simply not interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just confirmed that you made sure that a coroner was there who was supposed to do his job; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was all very fair and square. The usual procedure applied, the one that we had always applied, both before this incident and after. There is a procedure in place and everyone knows what the procedure is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Once you managed to get the truck ashore or as far as the edge of the river, would I be right to say that there were no plates on the truck?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: There was an inscription on the front door; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the telephone number that was written on the door?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a fax number and telephone number -- you're asking for too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever memorise those numbers?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a long number with many digits, not that easy to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Indeed. Nevertheless, in one of these documents that we are using here, we come across a reference to you providing both the fax and the telephone numbers. Would I be right in saying that the allegation that you actually knew that and could inform others about these numbers is true?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, quite the contrary, it is true. I wrote them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, no, I think you're misunderstanding my point. Yes, of course you made a note about those at the time but when you were subsequently prompted about the telephone number who did you share this with?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I produced a piece of paper, and I gave it to the Working Group --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So it was them, the Working Group, that you gave this to; right?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told the Working Group the telephone number and the fax number, and this can be seen on the photograph when it's enlarged, but certainly I hadn't memorised it. It's as if you were to ask me whether I know the telephone number of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: That is why I'm asking you because I thought it strange. Tell me, what other documents did you hand over to the Working Group?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just handed over the films, not the photographs, the negatives -- no, I'm sorry, maybe I gave them the photographs as well. I'm not sure. I gave them the negatives. I think I also gave them the photographs or maybe I tore them up, but I did give them the negatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have any evidence that you handed over to the Working Groups the film, you mean the developed film as we would say no normal vernacular, you handed over the film?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took out the film and developed it as early as 1999, and to my misfortune, this piece of film I kept in a drawer for two years; and it was only later when all this happened I gave them both the film and the photographs. Because in addition to these shots on this 36-picture film I took some other photographs as well during my normal duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Radojkovic, my question was: Did you receive anything that could be used as evidence that you had handed over this film to the Working Group?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think I was given anything, but later on when I handed over some other documents, then in that receipt it was indicated that among other things I had handed over those photographs, the film, as well as some other material.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, what happened next when the investigating judge of the municipal court said he was not competent and you informed the district public prosecutor and the investigating judge, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the investigating judge of the municipal court left the scene, everything was closed. The police stayed there to secure the site. I think that after that the truck was pulled further onto the bank, because I must explain that the level of the water varied because of the power-plant. So we pulled out the truck to dry land and then the next day it was already in water because the water-level changes. The shore is shallow there. So everything was closed, darkness started to fall. The crane was moved from the road several times for traffic to be able to pass so as to avoid a large column being formed, and we would let the vehicles and the buses pass. And then in the evening we went to the police station and then we talked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court usher, if possible --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: No, let me ask you something first. Am I right when I say that in the official note it is wrongly stated that Chief Sperlic came to the site and that he told you that everything had to be concealed on that second day?

utterances.speaker: BOSKO RADOJKOVIC [Resumed]
